clue.text: One urged to come home holding article of the Far East …

indicators.note: holding means the girl's name wraps round the article, which sits inside it

parts.note: Cathy Come Home was a famous 1966 BBC television play, so the girl urged to come home is Cathy
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Someone begged to return home is clutching some item from the Orient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cathy Come Home' was a landmark British TV play about homelessness. CATHY with A inside gives the old poetic name for China; the ellipsis carries the scene on into 4 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Cathay is the medieval European name, from Marco Polo's era, for China, the heart of the Far East.

clue.text: Worn out hero of Balaclava Bay?

definitions.text: Worn out hero of Balaclava Bay

parts.words: Worn out hero of Balaclava Bay
parts.note: a knitted jacket that is worn, named after the earl who led the Light Brigade at Balaclava, and also a Welsh bay

explanation.surface: An exhausted war hero from a bay at Balaclava.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worn out' looks like 'exhausted'; it means a garment worn outside. The Earl who led the Charge of the Light Brigade at Balaclava gave his name to it, and to a bay in west Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: The knitted button-up jacket is named after the 7th Earl of the same title, who led the Light Brigade.

parts.note: a jailer's job consists of twisting a key to lock and unlock cells

explanation.surface: A goalkeeper's straightforward procedure, an open-and-shut case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open and shut' looks like 'simple'; it is literal: the jailer's work is locking and unlocking doors.
explanation.definitionFit: A jailer is so named because they turn the key in the cell doors.

clue.text: Peter Pan players billed before Hair?

indicators.note: before means the first piece is placed ahead of the second

parts.note: AC is the abbreviation for account, and a billed item goes on account
tresses are long locks of hair

explanation.surface: Performers in Peter Pan advertised ahead of the musical Hair.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Pan is traditionally played on the British stage by a woman, so the players are female performers.
explanation.definitionFit: The boy hero of Peter Pan has long been played by a woman, so its players are female stage performers.

parts.note: read on from 1 across: a native of the Far East, and also a kind of ball bowled at Lord's, the cricket ground the quotation marks point to

explanation.surface: Following on from the Far East, it asks where some grand, lordly consignment originates.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is London's great cricket ground, so a 'lordly' delivery is a cricket ball bowled; the chinaman is a left-arm wrist-spinner's delivery. The ellipsis ties it to Cathay, home of a man from China.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a chinaman is a left-arm unorthodox spin ball, and the old term also meant a person from China.

clue.text: Formidable pair said to be moved to get things done

definitions.text: Formidable pair said to be moved to get things done

parts.words: Formidable pair said to be moved to get things done
parts.note: the idiom says someone will 'move' this sky-and-ground pair to achieve a goal

explanation.surface: A powerful duo who are reportedly shifted to make progress.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom is to move these two to do everything possible; 'formidable pair' disguises the sky and the world below.
explanation.definitionFit: To shift the sky and the world itself means to make every possible effort, as the idiom puts it.

parts.note: Eve suggests Adam's wife but means evening, which is followed by the dark hours when bats fly

explanation.surface: A dark-coloured bat trails after the first woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eve' looks like the woman of Genesis; it is evening, which precedes the dark time when bats come out.
explanation.definitionFit: The dark hours come after evening, and bats are creatures of that dark time.

definitions.meaning: to have fixed something on a support or backing, as a picture or gem
on horseback, as soldiers of the cavalry are

explanation.surface: Arranged in the manner of the horse soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: A jewel fixed in a setting and a soldier on horseback share the same past participle.

parts.note: the Head looks like a headmaster, but it is the body part bobbed down and up to show assent

explanation.surface: Concurred with the headmaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Head' looks like a headteacher; it is literally the head, bobbed to say yes.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick bob of the head is how people signal assent.

parts.note: inclined means bent or leaning
planes are trees, such as the London plane

explanation.surface: Asks what machine forces lie in crooked trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mechanical powers' is the old name for the simple machines (lever, wedge, screw and so on), one of which is a sloping surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloping surfaces are one of the classical simple machines, once called the mechanical powers.

clue.text: Romantic state of Mr Hawkins' imagination

definitions.text: Romantic state of Mr Hawkins' imagination

parts.words: Romantic state of Mr Hawkins' imagination
parts.note: Anthony Hope Hawkins, writing as Anthony Hope, invented a swashbuckling Central European kingdom for The Prisoner of Zenda

explanation.surface: A dreamy mood that a man called Hawkins conjured up in his mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Romantic state' looks like a mood; it is a fictional country. Mr Hawkins is the novelist better known as Anthony Hope.
explanation.definitionFit: The imaginary kingdom of The Prisoner of Zenda has become a byword for any picturesque, intrigue-filled little country.

parts.note: the hard rind of a certain fruit, dried and hollowed out, serves as a flask

explanation.surface: A bottle with fruit on the outside of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'bottle' is not glass at all but the dried shell of the fruit itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Dried hollowed squash-family fruits have long been used as water flasks, so the fruit's outer shell is the bottle.

clue.text: Whence a scholar may make his mark

definitions.text: Whence a scholar may make his mark

parts.words: Whence a scholar may make his mark
parts.note: a pupil dips a pen into a desk's ink pot before writing, literally making a mark

explanation.surface: Where a learned person might achieve distinction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make his mark' suggests fame; here it is a literal mark in ink, drawn from the pot set in an old school desk.
explanation.definitionFit: Old school desks held a small ink pot for pupils to dip pens in, the source of their written marks.

definitions.meaning: to grant someone a claim or permission
to call a book or work by a title

explanation.surface: Give a correct name.
explanation.definitionFit: To grant a claim and to bestow a title on a book are both senses of the same verb, built on 'title'.

parts.note: the clue quotes a Wordsworth line with its final word missing, and the solver supplies that word

explanation.surface: A line of Wordsworth's poetry with its last word left blank to fill in.
explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: the printed page shows a dash after 'dark', and the missing word from Wordsworth's line is a deep pit or gulf.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word names a bottomless chasm, the dark void the poet imagines at Nature's depths.

clue.text: When high is low in the main

definitions.text: When high is low in the main

parts.words: When high is low in the main
parts.note: 'the main' is the open sea, and 'high' is high water, which reaches its least height at a certain point of the moon's cycle

explanation.surface: Sounds like a remark about prices or spirits being down, on the whole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the main' looks like 'mostly'; it means at sea. High water is at its lowest at the tide that follows the moon's quarters.
explanation.definitionFit: At the moon's first and third quarters the tidal range is smallest, so even high water stays comparatively low.

clue.text: Youth is America's oldest according to Wilde

definitions.text: Youth is America's oldest according to Wilde

parts.words: Youth is America's oldest according to Wilde
parts.note: Oscar Wilde quipped that the youth of America is their oldest custom, running for three hundred years

explanation.surface: Oscar Wilde's witty remark about American youthfulness.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilde wrote in A Woman of No Importance that 'the youth of America is their oldest' custom; the clue drops the final word for the solver to supply.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilde's paradox calls American youthfulness its longest-standing inherited custom.

clue.text: Little bit crafty about being short in weight

indicators.note: about means the word for crafty goes round the other piece

parts.note: sly means crafty or cunning
light means short in weight

explanation.surface: A slightly cunning person seems to be giving underweight measures.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something to a small degree is to do it only a touch.

clue.text: Cut and took partners, without a good balance

parts.note: to lop is to cut off a branch
to have sided with someone is to have taken their part, joining them as partners

explanation.surface: At a dance, someone cut in and chose partners, losing their footing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something uneven, heavier on one side than the other, lacks a steady equilibrium.

parts.note: the word not is read as nought, O, a zero
standing means rating or rank

explanation.surface: Asks whether someone is speechifying in spite of everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notwithstanding' splits into 'not with standing': O (nothing) with RATING (standing).
explanation.definitionFit: Giving a long speech is delivering a formal address, holding the floor.

definitions.meaning: the month the rhyme 'Thirty days hath September' lists among those with thirty days

explanation.surface: A woman is sentenced to a month in prison.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a girl's name and the fourth month, which the old rhyme credits with thirty days.

clue.text: Train me to alter old clothes

indicators.note: to alter means the letters of the preceding words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Teaching me how to adjust hand-me-down garments.
explanation.definitionFit: Raiment is an old-fashioned literary word for garments.

parts.note: the press is a crowd crushing together, not journalists, and a crush of people is counted by how tightly they pack

explanation.surface: Tallying newspaper activity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The press' looks like journalists; it is a pressing crowd, whose activity is to crush together. The word also names a racket game where points are counted.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressing hard together in a crowd is to crush or squeeze, and the same word names a racket game scored by counting points.

definitions.meaning: a square-headed bolt shot from a crossbow
to argue and break off friendly relations

explanation.surface: A rocket drops away.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossbow bolt and a row between friends share one spelling.

indicators.note: sound means a word said aloud is heard as another spelling

parts.note: rain is wet weather

explanation.surface: Gold coins sound damp, it exclaims.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sovereigns' looks like gold coins; it means monarchs, and what monarchs do sounds like falling water from the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Monarchs rule, which is the verb for holding royal power.

parts.note: a rising is a rebellion or uprising

explanation.surface: An uprising is on its way.
explanation.definitionFit: To emerge or appear is to occur or get up, as a problem or sleeper does.

clue.text: Means to prove what makes the heart grow fonder

definitions.text: Means to prove what makes the heart grow fonder

parts.words: Means to prove what makes the heart grow fonder
parts.note: the proverb says absence makes the heart grow fonder, so this is a way of proving one was absent from a crime scene

explanation.surface: A way to show what deepens love.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'absence makes the heart grow fonder' supplies the hidden word absence: a plea that one was elsewhere at the time.
explanation.definitionFit: A suspect's defence that they were somewhere else proves their absence from the crime.

parts.note: 'the Diet' looks like a parliament such as Japan's, but it is food, and its constitution is what it is made of

explanation.surface: The founding charter of a national assembly.
explanation.walkthrough: A Diet is a parliament (Japan's, or the old German imperial one), so 'constitution' looks political; really it is what a diet consists of.
explanation.definitionFit: Nourishment is the substance any diet is made up of.

parts.note: exalted means high in rank
Loch Ness in Scotland is the fabled home of the Loch Ness monster

explanation.surface: The street address of some lofty creature's dwelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Address' is a form of address, the style used to speak to a prince or princess.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Your Highness' is the formal way to address royalty, so the title is a form of address.

clue.text: Does the reefer pose such a problem ?

definitions.text: Does the reefer pose such a problem

parts.words: Does the reefer pose such a problem
parts.note: a reefer is a reef knot, and a tangled difficulty is described as full of knots

explanation.surface: Asks whether a cannabis cigarette creates this kind of difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: A reefer looks like a joint of cannabis; here it is the sailor's reef knot, and a hard problem is said to be knotted.
explanation.definitionFit: A tricky, intricate problem is called tangled, like a rope full of knots.
